passage:
Wednesday. Finished the report at five thirty. Kavitha Ma'am and the seniors were still at their desks, so I opened old emails and pretended to work until eight. Nobody asked me to stay. I just couldn't be the first one out and look lazy. The bus was full and the dinner was cold when I got home.
Lying here I keep thinking: what does Ma'am actually see? A chair filled after hours. She hasn't even opened my report.
Tomorrow I will send the report at five thirty, with a two-line summary, and ask if she needs anything else before I go. If that feels wrong, I will ask her what she prefers. Better to be judged on the work than on the chair.
Yogesh

qa.a: Yogesh finished the report at five thirty.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling while staying at the desk until eight?
qa.a: Yogesh felt anxious about looking lazy and pressured to copy the seniors, even though the work was done.

qa.q: What plan does Yogesh make for the next day?
qa.a: Yogesh will send the report at five thirty with a short summary and ask Ma'am if anything else is needed before leaving, so results speak louder than presence.

qa.q: What might Kavitha Ma'am actually be noticing about the late-staying juniors?
qa.a: She may notice a filled chair, as Yogesh guesses, but she has not opened the report, so she may be judging the work less than the presence.

grounding: A new hire stays after hours to look committed though the work is done, then plans to show results and set honest limits.

passage:
In his first job at a Madrid consultancy, Tomas, twenty-two, noticed that nobody left before eight. So he stayed too, even on days his work was done by five. He'd reorganise folders, reread emails, anything to look busy.
His colleague Ines left at six every day. At first Tomas thought she wasn't serious.
After two months, he was exhausted and snapping at his flatmates. Then the quarterly review came. Ines had closed two client projects early; her reports were the clearest on the team. Tomas's work was fine, but he'd missed a deadline because he was so tired.
At lunch, he asked her how she did it. Ines shrugged. "I do the work, and then I go home. My results speak. If I'm needed late, I stay."
Tomas left at six the next day. His heart raced as he walked out, but nobody said a word.

qa.q: What time did Ines leave every day?
qa.a: Ines left at six every day.

qa.q: What was Tomas feeling as he walked out at six?
qa.a: Tomas felt nervous, his heart racing, afraid of looking less committed.

qa.q: What did Tomas learn from Ines?
qa.a: He learned that clear results and honest limits prove commitment better than just being visible late in the office.

qa.q: How might Ines see Tomas's long hours?
qa.a: Ines probably sees them as unnecessary, since she believes results speak louder than presence.

grounding: Outside India, a new hire stays late to look committed though his work is done, and learns from a colleague that results and honest limits are better proof.

passage:
At the bank branch in Indore, Charu, twenty-one, had finished her ledger by six. But her senior, Sonali Ma'am, was still at her desk, so Charu stayed. Everyone did. It was how you showed you were serious.
For a month, Charu reached home at nine, too tired to eat. She started making small mistakes in the mornings.
One evening, the branch manager walked past. "Charu, why are you still here? Is something pending?"
"No, sir. I just..."
"Then go home. I don't count hours. I count accurate ledgers." He turned to Sonali Ma'am. "You too."
Sonali Ma'am laughed, embarrassed. "Habit."
Walking to the bus stop, Charu felt strangely light. The next day, she finished by six, checked her work twice, and left, saying a polite good night to everyone.

qa.q: What time had Charu finished her ledger?
qa.a: Charu had finished her ledger by six.

qa.q: How was Charu feeling during the month she stayed late?
qa.a: Charu felt exhausted, too tired to eat, and began making small mistakes.

qa.q: What did the branch manager's words teach Charu?
qa.a: He showed that accurate work, not hours spent sitting, is what counts, so honest limits are fine.

qa.q: How might Sonali Ma'am feel when the manager tells her to go home too?
qa.a: Sonali Ma'am seemed embarrassed, realising her late hours were just habit.

grounding: A new hire stays late because seniors do, though her work is done, and learns that results and honest limits are better proof than presence.

passage:
Dear Amandeep,
You asked about my first job. Honestly, I'm tired all the time, and it's my own fault.
Everyone on my team stays till nine. So I do too. Even when my reports are done by five-thirty. I sit there pretending to type, scared that if I leave, they'll think I'm lazy.
Last week my manager said in my review, "Your work is good, but it has errors on Mondays." I know why. I've been sleeping five hours a night.
I watched one senior, Mr. Rao, leave at six every day. Everyone respects him. His work is excellent. I asked him how. He said, "Nobody remembers who stayed late. They remember who delivered."
So I'm trying: finish well, send a short update to my manager, and go home. Yesterday was the first time. I felt guilty for about ten minutes, then I ate dinner with my family.
Reena

qa.q: What did Reena's manager say in her review?
qa.a: Reena's manager said, "Your work is good, but it has errors on Mondays."

qa.q: How does Reena feel about staying late?
qa.a: Reena feels tired all the time and scared that leaving early will make others think Reena lazy.

qa.q: What is Reena trying now, and why does it help?
qa.a: Reena finishes the work well, sends a short update to the manager and goes home, letting results rather than presence show her commitment.

qa.q: How might Mr. Rao see Reena's late nights?
qa.a: Mr. Rao would probably see them as unnecessary, since he believes people remember who delivered, not who stayed late.

grounding: A new hire stays late to look committed though her work is done, and learns from a senior that results and honest limits are better proof.
